opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly my thinking has changed a lot over the years.

When I started my PhD, I didn't think much about "impact" in an abstract sense. I mostly worked on things that bothered me. With XGBoost, for example, I wanted to run gradient boosting fast and at scale, and the tools I had weren't good enough. So I built something for myself first. It turned out a lot of other people had the same problem, and that's where the impact came from.

So one lesson I took away is that real impact usually comes from solving a real problem, ideally one you feel yourself. If you're a user of your own system, you get very honest feedback very quickly.

The second thing I think about is where the field is going, not just where it is today. With TVM and machine learning compilation, the bet was that models and hardware would both keep diversifying, so you'd need a more systematic way to bring models onto all kinds of devices. At the time it wasn't obvious that compilers were the right answer. But if you think a few years out and ask what will become a bottleneck, you can sometimes position yourself to work on the thing that matters when everyone else gets there.

The third piece is the full stack. A lot of research impact comes from carrying an idea all the way through: from the paper to an open-source system people can actually use, then to a community that keeps it alive. I've found that the last mile, making things usable and building the community, is often where most of the impact is, even though it's not always rewarded in the traditional academic sense.

Finally, I try not to over-optimize for expected impact, because it's very hard to predict. Some of the most important things I've worked on started as side projects or felt a bit risky. So I'd say: pick problems you genuinely care about, have a hypothesis about why they'll matter in the future, and then be willing to go deep and actually build the thing. If you do that consistently, impact tends to follow.

r001.rationale: The response says research impact is hard to predict, but does not say it is difficult to measure.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says impact is “very hard to predict.”

r003.rationale: It recommends choosing problems you genuinely care about and describes starting with problems that bothered him personally.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I'm a bit suspicious of the phrase "expected impact," because when I look back at the projects that ended up mattering most, I don't think I could have predicted their impact at the start. XGBoost began as me wanting a faster, more scalable tree booster for my own experiments. TVM started from frustration that every new hardware backend meant rewriting operators by hand. Neither of those felt like a grand bet on the future. They felt like concrete problems that I personally had and that nobody had solved well.

So the way I actually think about it has a few pieces.

First, I ask whether the problem is real and whether I can feel it myself. If I'm the user of the thing I'm building, I get very fast feedback about what matters and what's just an abstraction I invented. A lot of research is motivated by a problem the author has only read about, and you can tell, because the solution optimizes the wrong thing.

Second, I look for places where the abstraction is wrong or missing. Impactful systems work is often less about a clever algorithm and more about finding the right layer to insert yourself. If you can define a boundary that lets many people above it stop worrying about what's below it, that tends to compound. Compilers, runtimes, and libraries all live at those boundaries. The question I ask is, if this works, how many people's lives get simpler, and do they have to change much to benefit.

Third, I think about timing. Machine learning hardware and models are moving fast, so the question isn't only "is this important" but "is this important in two or three years, when the project is actually mature." Sometimes the right move is to build the infrastructure before the demand is obvious, as long as you can see the trend line. That's a bet, and you'll be wrong sometimes, but being early on a real trend is where most of the leverage is.

And finally, I care a lot about whether the project can grow beyond me. Open source has shaped how I think here. If the only way the thing has impact is through my own hands, the ceiling is low. If I can build it so a community can take it further, make it their own, extend it in directions I wouldn't have thought of, then the expected impact is really the sum of all those people's work, not mine. So I try to choose problems where that kind of ecosystem can form.

Put together, I'd say I don't optimize for expected impact directly. I pick concrete problems I actually have, at a layer where the abstraction is broken, on a trend that's clearly coming, and I build them in a way others can own. The impact tends to follow, but usually in a shape I didn't anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether impact can be predicted, but does not state that research impact is difficult to measure.

r002.rationale: It says the projects that mattered most were not ones whose impact the speaker could have predicted at the start.

r003.rationale: It recommends choosing concrete problems the speaker personally experiences and says personal feedback helps identify what matters.

astra-6.text:
I think about impact as a useful guide, but not something you can predict precisely at the beginning. You can ask: If this project succeeds, who would care? What would they be able to do that they cannot do today? That helps make the ambition concrete.

But I also look at what we can learn along the way. A project might have a very exciting potential outcome, but if there is no clear first step, it is hard to make progress. I like to find a small experiment that can tell us whether the direction is promising, then update our thinking based on what happens.

So I would balance a long-term vision with a short-term learning process. Have a reason to believe the problem matters, but stay open to discovering that the most useful contribution is different from what you initially imagined.

r001.rationale: The response says impact cannot be predicted precisely, but does not say it is difficult to measure.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says impact cannot be predicted precisely at the beginning.

r003.rationale: It discusses project impact and learning, but does not endorse personal interest as a basis for choosing projects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think expected impact is useful, but it’s very hard to estimate at the beginning of a research project. You have uncertainty about whether the idea will work, but also about whether you’re solving the right problem.

So I would start by asking: if we solve this problem, what does it enable people to do? Does it remove a bottleneck? Could the solution be useful beyond the particular example we’re studying? Then I’d look for a small experiment that helps us test those assumptions.

I also think you need to leave room for curiosity. If you only work on things whose impact is already obvious, you may miss something important. For me, it’s a balance between having a meaningful direction and being willing to change your understanding as you learn.

r001.rationale: The response says expected impact is hard to estimate at the beginning, but does not state that research impact is difficult to measure.

r002.rationale: It says expected impact is very hard to estimate at the beginning and describes uncertainty about whether the idea will work or address the right problem.

r003.rationale: It endorses leaving room for curiosity when choosing projects, which communicates personal interest as one basis for research.
